KEYLESS CAR THEFT

By: Nicky Troll | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Car thieves evolve – swopping guns for clever technology to steal your wheels is the latest MO knocking high-end car across the country.

Unique Selling Point:
- new car theft trend
- cctv footage

Summary:
If it wasn’t a hijacking, Keyless Entry Cars have been relatively safe from theft…. Until recently. Car Criminals have upgraded their skills and technology using specialist device to target high end vehicles without having to physically challenge the driver.

Further information:
BACKGROUND
It’s not really a new trend – globally car thieves have been making off with high-end vehicles like this for years. South Africans criminals are new to the MO and are making up for lost times.

Year on year – insurers say there’s a definite spike in keyless-go cars being stolen. Armed with high-tech devices these criminals are working over time – targeting the pricey makes - the average value of a stolen vehicle increase by more than 75% in just the last year!
Local insurers and vehicle manufacturers are scrambling for solutions. It’s a constant race between automotive engineers and criminals.

When cars come out with new technologies to beef up their security features, it usually takes criminals about a year to crack how to bypass those technologies. Sometimes, these syndicates are assisted by people who have worked in the industry before.
HOW DO THEY DO IT?
It started in eastern and western Europe a at least 4-5 years ago.
Criminals carry devices that amplify the sensor of the car keys. One follows the driver to pick up their key signal and boost it to the parking lot where their accomplice waits, even if the driver is inside a shopping mall or sleeping inside their house. And because keyless-entry cars allow their owners to open the door and start the ignition without the physical key, criminals can drive away for many kilometres until they reach a "safe house", where they then re-program the key or replace the ignition altogether.
There are three basic MO’s relay theft, CAN bus theft and the last one involves some force as they break a window to gain access. We’ll brief cover the MO’s without getting bogged down by the detail.
SOLUTIONS?
While manufacturers are working on solutions around the clock, the only temporary solution is a special pouch that blocks the signal being duplicated. The Insurance Crime Bureau have nabbed one of the gangs and have recovered some of the devices that are being used to reverse engineer solutions – Toyota is making significant progress on the matter and have agreed to an interview because they have been knocked quite hard by this MO as a brand.
WE HAVE FOOTAGE OF SOME OF THE INCIDENTS – LOCALLY AND INTERNATIONALLY

CASE STUDY TBC CONFIRMED – Might need be hidden ID – have spoken to two that don’t want to be on camera – but I’m on a mission today to lock them in.

VO: A car stolen every 13 minutes; more than 100 each day .

LINK: Broad daylight public spaces. Not a gun in sight. Yet criminals are cracking intricate vehicle security systems and making off with cars in just seconds.

VO: High-end Keyless Entry vehicles are in demand. Especially on the black market for stolen cars.

LIEB: if a vehicle is needed in a market, they will take it.

VO: The latest Modus Operandi is linked to sophisticated syndicates. Louwrens Liebenberg is from the Insurance Crime Bureau.

LIEB: Opportunistic car thieves have been taken out of the equation a long time ago through technology. We are left with criminals that are focused and they are one step ahead and they've got very good technology

VO: You park your car in a busy area, thinking it safe - but it’s not, it’s more vulnerable than ever. This new car theft trend is taking old school breaking and entering to a whole new level.

FRITZ: In my wildest dreams, I never thought it was be possible

VO: Fritz Stols parked at a shopping centre in his top of the range double cab - only to return a short while later, and find his bakkie, was gone.

FRITZ: I thought I parked it somewhere else. // I specifically stopped the car at a busy place so that they don't smash and grab me, steal my stuff. And then they stole the whole thing.

VO: The bakkie was taken in seconds without having the car key.

LINK: With jamming attacks, we've become extra vigilant, making double, if not triple, sure that the car is locked before you walk away. But that won't cut it with this latest car theft trend.

MATTHEW: // All models that have wireless key systems are now being affected because//. It's actually effortless with the right equipment.

VO: But just how are tech savvy criminals getting around complex vehicle security systems?

Matthew Parker is a vehicle security inventor. He’s built a demo unit to help us better understand how criminals are stealing keyless entry cars - that’s the future!

So the vulnerability is that I'm amplifying the signal. So this laptop and bag is going to follow you into the shops. I'm then going to pick up this wireless key signal and boost it back to the vehicle. I'm not cloning the key. I'm purely amplifying the signal of the key itself.

MATTHEW: // All I need to do is come with the receiver. And as soon as I touch the handles, because it's a wireless model, I can jump in. And if I do jump into the vehicle and it picks up the wireless key, I'm able to start it.

MATTHEW: // Once the car’s started, obviously, I'm going to have to deal with the unfortunate thing of a tracker potentially being in the vehicle. So what I utilize is a piece of equipment that looks like this. This is called the signal Jammer. And all I have to do is turn it on, put it on the seat, and off I go.
CLAIRE: Easy like that, guys just gone

LIEB: // it's easy for them to blend in // You will not notice that they are following you with amplifying device //you will think it's a laptop bag or eye or a backpack that is being carried on on daily use. You will not notice this guy.

VO: It’s a well orchestrated crime carried out using three main MO’s

In all scenarios, the car's starter motor is not damaged and the thieves don’t physically challenge the driver.

In this next clip, focus on the Fortuner, there’s a man to the right of the screen, hovering while the driver gets out - look at him talking on his phone, then tying his shoe. He’s waiting for the driver to lock and go about his business. As he walks in behind the driver, a second thief moves in - opens the car and just like that another keyless car theft is pulled off in seconds.

While this trend is relatively new to South Africa, car thieves globally have been at it since 2017, and it seems local syndicates are making up for lost time.

LIEB: // There is no one big syndicate that's running everything. You get your Crews // working on a daily basis. // they will take up to five, five, six vehicles per day in a certain area. And they will operate, say, for five days a week. You can work out how many they are taking.

VO: Conservatively, 200 luxury keyless entry cars are stolen every month in and around Gauteng alone - the majority of these, are destined for the cross-border market.

LIEB: Unfortunately, if a recipe out //they will apply that recipe. And it's an easy way now that they've uncovered how to steal these vehicles // And there's a market for these vehicles, //.

VO: We made a couple of enquiries at local tech stores, and managed to get an actual quote for the devices used by criminals.

But as easy as that was, car thieves should beware: if they're caught with any of these gadgets, they won't just face theft charges, the crime is being redefined.

LIEB: // other legislation might be applicable like the Cyber Crimes Act, because you are actually interfering with a computer system when you interfere with a system like this on a vehicle.

VO: These syndicates even use technology to cover their tracks - they come armed with signal jammers to prevent tracking companies from locating the cars.

MATTHEW: //If I turn this on, it will blank this entire area. //It will shield the car from any radio interference. So the tracker might be trying to send out a signal. But there is so much noise behind it that it's not able to.

MATTHEW: //it'll take about 30 minutes to code in a new key into the vehicle// So that's that's the biggest weak point is time. And when you can reduce that, you can reduce the risk of vehicle theft.

FRITZ: Look how that worked out for me. //I always thought they going to put it on a fla tbed and drive it away, but never thought they going to steal actually the whole thing.

VO: Looking at the CCTV footage of the theft, Stols is still stunned.

CLAIRE: //my heart would be pounding
FRITZ: I almost cried. I am cried. I couldnt believe it.

VO: Watch as Stols gets out of the bakkie and walks away, a man heads in his direction and appears to also go into the shops. You wouldn’t think anything of it…. until that same man comes back seconds later.

FRITZ: 30 seconds. …. 30 seconds.
CLAIRE: My heart is breaking. Like it's happening now.
FRITZ: I was flabbergasted, It's not the first ranger they stole. You can see it's clearly professionals.

VO: Once they’ve got the signal – it’s game over. They’re in and driving off without the actual key.

MATTHEW: The manufacturer should be investigating a fix t// what this car is, it's basically a computer on wheels. So they're able to modify the code and change the the specifications of the vehicle, which I think is a demand in South Africa at the moment.

VO: Manufacturers are taking up the challenge and fighting back against these car thieves turned hackers.

By collaborating with local law enforcement and Japanese design teams - Theron and his colleagues are taking an out of the box approach - even turning to some shady operators to test their latest security upgrades.

LEON: We got people. In. To say, okay, well, this work. And then they found another way to get into the vehicle. So we then had to enhance that as well. So it's been a quite a long process It took us literally 12 months to get to where we are now. We we feel a lot more secure M12

VO: They will be rolling out the updated features in new models and offering current owners an in dealership solution.

While Ford South Africa declined an interview - they stated they too continuously invest in security measures and are adopting new techniques to develop solutions to deter vehicle related crimes.

And while manufacturers are gearing up to roll out new security features, Parker has a security tweak of his own that will hopefully hamper car thieves.

MATTHEW: // The system that I developed. Reverses the roles between the car and the keys. So instead of the car always asking for the keys signal, I then make the key request for the car signal I1M12 begin

VO: There are also a few low tech solutions on the market from the gearlock of years gone by to frequency blocking key pouches.

MATTHEW: as soon as you've locked the car. You can put the key in a little pouch and as soon as you walk off, it creates what's called a Faraday cage and it will block this key from transmitting.

VO: As car thieves evolve and adapt their ways, additional measures to secure your keyless car are becoming non-negotiable, if you want to avoid becoming a statistic.

MATTHEW: / if you don't have anything fitted on your car, I would be exceptionally worried at the shops.

VO: It’s a constant race between automotive engineers and criminals - when manufacturers launch new security features, syndicates take roughly a year to crack and bypass those technologies.

metadata.Summary: If it wasn’t a hijacking, Keyless Entry Cars have been relatively safe from theft…. Until recently. Car Criminals have upgraded their skills and technology using specialist device to target high end vehicles without having to physically challenge the driver.
metadata.Further information: BACKGROUND It’s not really a new trend – globally car thieves have been making off with high-end vehicles like this for years. South Africans criminals are new to the MO and are making up for lost times. Year on year – insurers say there’s a definite spike in keyless-go cars being stolen. Armed with high-tech devices these criminals are working over time – targeting the pricey makes - the average value of a stolen vehicle increase by more than 75% in just the last year! Local insurers and vehicle manufacturers are scrambling for solutions. It’s a constant race between automotive engineers and criminals. When cars come out with new technologies to beef up their security features, it usually takes criminals about a year to crack how to bypass those technologies. Sometimes, these syndicates are assisted by people who have worked in the industry before. HOW DO THEY DO IT? It started in eastern and western Europe a at least 4-5 years ago. Criminals carry devices that amplify the sensor of the car keys. One follows the driver to pick up their key signal and boost it to the parking lot where their accomplice waits, even if the driver is inside a shopping mall or sleeping inside their house. And because keyless-entry cars allow their owners to open the door and start the ignition without the physical key, criminals can drive away for many kilometres until they reach a "safe house", where they then re-program the key or replace the ignition altogether. There are three basic MO’s relay theft, CAN bus theft and the last one involves some force as they break a window to gain access. We’ll brief cover the MO’s without getting bogged down by the detail. SOLUTIONS? While manufacturers are working on solutions around the clock, the only temporary solution is a special pouch that blocks the signal being duplicated. The Insurance Crime Bureau have nabbed one of the gangs and have recovered some of the devices that are being used to reverse engineer solutions – Toyota is making significant progress on the matter and have agreed to an interview because they have been knocked quite hard by this MO as a brand.
